About: Refraction — Why the Ray Bends, and Why the Pool Looks Shallow

Source

Topic
Geometric optics — refraction at a flat interface
Concept
The ray bends because one side of the wavefront is slowed before the other; the same slowing raises the apparent depth of a submerged object.
Audience
JEE (NCERT Class 11–12): Snell's law, refractive index, apparent depth.
Serves
Mechanism-first understanding of refraction; connects two textbook results (bending toward the normal; d′ = d/n) to a single cause (slower light in the denser medium).
Inquiry
What happens to the bending at exactly normal incidence — bends most, bends least, or not at all?
Misconception
“Light bends because the water pushes it,” or “refraction is a property of the ray, not the wave.” The pivoting wavefront makes both wrong.

Refraction
The mechanism — wavefront crossing a slower medium
The consequence — coin at the bottom of a pool

Guided Inquiry

The setup

A ray of light in air strikes the flat surface of water at some angle. In water, light travels slower — that single fact drives everything you're about to see. On the left, the ray arrives at 45° and leaves the surface on a new line; the dashed grey line is where it would have gone had it not bent.

Angles are measured from the normal — the dashed line perpendicular to the surface.

Predict: normal incidence

Now suppose the ray comes straight down — perpendicular to the surface, angle of incidence = 0°. What happens to the bending?

The mechanism — a pivoting wavefront

The blue bars are wavefronts — surfaces where the wave is in step. In air they march forward at c. The moment one end of a bar enters water it slows; the other end is still in air moving at full speed. The bar pivots, and the whole wave now points in a new direction — bent toward the normal.

Move the incidence slider between 60° and 0°. At 60° the pivot is dramatic. At 0° both ends enter together and nothing pivots.

The consequence — the pool looks shallow

Look at the right panel. A coin sits on the bottom of a pool of real depth d. Rays from the coin bend away from the normal on their way out to your eye. Your brain ignores the bend — it extrapolates the outgoing rays back in a straight line, and they cross at a shallower apparent depth.

Change the Real depth. Notice: the apparent depth equals real depth ÷ n. For water, a 1 m pool looks about 0.75 m deep.

Two effects, one cause

Set the incidence angle to exactly 0°. On the left the bending has vanished. But the coin on the right still looks raised. Why?

Why the wavefront pivots
In a time Δt the end of the bar still in air travels v₁ Δt; the end already in water travels only v₂ Δt < v₁ Δt. The wavefront is the line joining the two ends, so it turns — and since the ray is perpendicular to the wavefront, so does the ray.

01

At a glance

A ray of light crosses the flat surface between air and a slower medium, while a coin lies on the bottom of a pool. The sim draws the wavefronts of the ray on the left and the view of the coin on the right, so you can look for one cause behind both.

What you'll learn

  • How the speed of light in a medium is linked to its refractive index.
  • How the angle on the air side is related to the angle in the medium, and what sets the bend.
  • How the apparent depth of a submerged object depends on its real depth and on the medium.
Left: the surface, the normal and the incoming ray. Right: the pool, the coin and the eye.

  • Wavefronts: blue bars across the ray, marching toward the surface when the sim runs.
  • Path with no bend: the grey dashed line the ray would follow if it did not change direction.
  • The coin: the real coin on the bottom, and a dashed blue ring where the eye places it.
  • Readouts: the refraction angle θ₂ and the apparent depth d′.

03

Light is slower in a denser medium

The refractive index n of a medium compares the speed of light in vacuum, c, with its speed v in the medium:

n = c / v   so   v = c / n
c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s. For air the sim uses n₁ = 1.00.
Mediumn₂v
Water1.332.254 × 10⁸ m/s
Glass1.501.999 × 10⁸ m/s
Diamond2.421.239 × 10⁸ m/s

The source fixes the frequency, so it is the same on both sides. A slower wave with the same frequency has a shorter wavelength, λ₂ = λ₁/n₂. The wavefronts below the surface sit closer together.

See itChoose diamond with the ray at 45°. Watch for: the blue bars below the surface packed much closer than those in air, about 2.4 times closer.
04

The wavefront pivots, so the ray bends

A wavefront reaches the surface at A. By the time its far end B reaches the surface at C, the end in air has covered BC = v₁Δt. Meanwhile the wavelet from A has gone only AD = v₂Δt in the slower medium. The new wavefront is CD, so the wave has turned.

The wave turns because one end of the wavefront is slowed first.

With AC the stretch of surface from A to C, sin θ₁ = v₁Δt/AC and sin θ₂ = v₂Δt/AC. Dividing, and using v = c/n:

n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Snell's law, with both angles measured from the normal.

If θ₁ = 0, the whole wavefront reaches the surface at once, so no end is slowed first and nothing pivots: θ₂ = 0.

See itSet θ₁ to 0°, then drag it up to 60°. Watch for: at 0° the refracted ray lying on the grey dashed line and θ₂ reading 0.00°. At 60° the bars pivot where they cross the surface.
05

A higher index bends the ray more

Entering the denser medium from air, Snell's law gives

sin θ₂ = sin θ₁ / n₂
n₂ is greater than 1, so θ₂ is always smaller than θ₁: the ray bends toward the normal.

The larger n₂ is, the smaller θ₂ is for the same θ₁. At θ₁ = 45°:

Mediumθ₂Bend, θ₁ − θ₂
Water, 1.3332.1°12.9°
Glass, 1.5028.1°16.9°
Diamond, 2.4217.0°28.0°

At the slider's top angle, 80°, θ₂ reaches only 47.8° in water, 41.0° in glass and 24.0° in diamond.

See itKeep θ₁ at 45° and switch the medium to diamond. Watch for: θ₂ reading 16.99° instead of 32.12° for water, and the refracted ray swung toward the normal.
06

The pool looks shallower by the factor n

Rays from the coin bend away from the normal as they leave the water. The eye follows them back in a straight line, and the lines cross higher than the coin. Seen from nearly straight above:

d′ = d / n
d is the real depth, d′ the apparent depth, n the index of the medium.

For a 1 m pool, d′ = 0.752 m in water, 0.667 m in glass and 0.413 m in diamond. Doubling d doubles d′. The formula uses small angles, so it holds for a view nearly vertical, which is why the sim notes that its angles are exaggerated.

The θ₁ slider does not enter. At θ₁ = 0 the left panel shows no bend, yet the coin still looks raised. Bending needs a tilted wavefront to pivot, while d′ depends on n alone. Both come from light being slower in the medium.

See itSet θ₁ to 0° and the depth to 2.00 m, in water. Watch for: no bend on the left, yet d′ reading 1.504 m on the right and the dashed ring well above the real coin.
07

Where it matters

  • Pools and streams. Seen from above, the bottom looks about a quarter shallower than it is, so the water is deeper than it looks.
  • A straw in a glass. The part under water looks bent at the surface, because the rays from it refract as they leave.
  • Diamond. With n = 2.42, light inside travels at 0.41 c, and rays hitting the surface from inside beyond 24.4° cannot leave. That trapping gives a cut diamond its sparkle.
Go deeper: one number per medium

A real medium has a slightly different n for each colour, which is how a prism splits white light. The sim uses one typical value for each medium, so it shows no colours.

08

Summary

In one line. Light travels at v = c/n in a medium, and this sim shows how that slowing sets the bend of a ray and the apparent depth of a coin.

Key points

  • v = c/n: light is slower where n is larger, with the same frequency and a shorter wavelength.
  • n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ follows from the pivoting wavefront. Angles are from the normal.
  • Entering a denser medium, the ray bends toward the normal, and more for a larger n.
  • d′ = d/n for a near-vertical view, whatever the angle of the ray on the left.

Common mix-ups

  • "The water pushes the light sideways." Nothing pushes. One end of the wavefront is slowed first, so the wave turns.
  • "Bending and the raised coin are two separate effects." They share one cause, but the bend needs a tilted wavefront and d′ does not.
  • "Angles are measured from the surface." Both θ₁ and θ₂ are measured from the normal.

Things to try on your own

  • In water, find the θ₁ that gives θ₂ close to 30°, then check it with n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
  • In diamond, find the smallest θ₁ at which θ₂ reaches 10°.
  • Choose glass, set d = 1.50 m, and check that d′ reads 1.000 m.
